slides.title: Distributed AMQP Messaging Cluster
script: Good morning. We are Group 4, and our project is a distributed AMQP messaging cluster built on RabbitMQ.

Our goal: when a broker node fails, no message that the broker has confirmed may be lost. [point at the orange line] We built a three-node cluster with Docker Compose, our own Python producer and consumer, Prometheus and Grafana monitoring, which is the bonus, and tests that check every message.
slides.point: The goal line, then the orange technology line, then the four role cards as you introduce the team.
slides.proves: Sets the goal the whole talk will prove: zero loss of confirmed messages during node failures.
slides.transition: Click straight to slide 2 and keep talking.

slides.title: Architecture: the four C4 diagrams
script: We modelled the system with all four levels of the C4 model.
[point at 1] The context: our cluster with the producer, the consumer, the validator, the operator and the dashboards around it.
[point at 2] The containers: three RabbitMQ 3.13.7 nodes sharing the Raft layer of our queue, plus Prometheus and Grafana.
[point at 3] The components: retry and failover, confirm tracking, acknowledgements and de-duplication in our clients, and the quorum queue with its Raft replica inside a node.
[point at 4] And the deployment: one Docker host, the ports, and a persistent volume per node.
slides.point: The numbered labels 1, 2, 3, 4 in order. Do not try to read the small boxes.
slides.numbers: Ports: 5672-5674 AMQP, 15672-15674 management, 15692 metrics, 9090 Prometheus, 3000 Grafana (only if asked).
slides.proves: All four C4 diagrams the assignment requires exist and match docker-compose.yml and the code.
slides.transition: "Now let me zoom into the cluster itself."

slides.title: Three nodes, one replicated quorum queue
script: Our queue, hw2.orders, is a quorum queue, copied to all three nodes with Raft: one leader and two followers.

The leader writes each message to its log and sends it to the followers. When two of the three have it on disk, it is committed, and only then is the producer's confirm sent. Three is the smallest cluster that keeps a majority after one failure.
[point at the list] pause_minority prevents a second leader, a full queue rejects instead of dropping, and each node keeps its Raft log on a volume.

[point at the screenshot] And here is our health check on Docker: three nodes running, no alarms, no partitions; the queue is quorum, its leader at that moment was rabbit3, and three of three members are online. Result: HEALTHY.
slides.point: The leader and follower boxes, the commit rule, the configuration list, then in the screenshot: the three True values, ALARMS none, quorum, rabbit3, 3/3, RESULT: HEALTHY.
slides.numbers: 2 of 3 = the Raft majority. 3/3 = all replicas of the queue online. Leader rabbit3 is just the leader at the time of the check; any node can lead.
slides.proves: The cluster runs on Docker with three healthy nodes and a fully replicated quorum queue, and we have a management tool that checks it.
slides.transition: Hand over to Person 2: "[P2 name] will now show how we monitor this cluster."

slides.title: Bonus: Prometheus + Grafana, verified on Docker
script: Thank you. The bonus asks for Prometheus and Grafana collecting queue depth, message rates and node health.

[point at the targets screenshot] Every RabbitMQ node exports metrics on port 15692. Prometheus scrapes them every five seconds, and here you can see all seven targets are UP: Prometheus itself, and two jobs on each of the three nodes.

[point at the large Grafana screenshot] This is our Grafana dashboard on Docker during a message-processing run. The publish, confirm, deliver and acknowledge rates rise together to about 500 messages per second, and the traffic is spread over all three nodes. The redelivered rate stays at zero.
[point at the queue panel] Below, the queue depth climbs to about 2,700 messages and drops back to zero as soon as the four consumers attach.

[point at the terminal] Finally, our script check_monitoring.py proves that this is more than running containers. It found Grafana up, the Prometheus data source and all three dashboards provisioned, and all 22 dashboard queries returning data through Grafana. Result: MONITORING CHECK PASS. We also wrote eight alert rules, all evaluating without errors.
slides.point: Targets: the three (n/n up) headings. Grafana: the four rate lines and the per-node panel. Queue panel: the peak and the drop, and the 4 consumers. Terminal: 22/22 and PASS.
slides.numbers: 7/7 = all scrape targets healthy. About 500 msg/s = the cluster-wide rate in that run. About 2.7 K = messages waiting before the consumers started. 22/22 = every panel query of our dashboard works through Grafana.
slides.proves: The bonus is implemented and working on our Docker stack: queue depth, message rates and node health are collected and displayed, and an automated check confirms it end to end.
slides.transition: "Next, [P3 name] explains how the producer makes sure messages are not lost on the way in."

slides.title: Producer: publisher confirms and failover
script: Thanks. [point at step 1] In our producer each thread has its own connection and channel, because pika objects are not thread-safe.

[point at the code] We turn on publisher confirms. Every message is persistent and has a unique message ID. With confirms on, basic_publish returns only after the broker has confirmed the message, and for a quorum queue that means it is on two of the three disks.

If the broker answers with a nack, for example because the queue is full, we retry up to five times. If the connection breaks before the confirm arrives, we cannot know whether the message was stored, so we send it again with the same ID. That can create a duplicate, but never a loss.

[point at the bottom line] Reconnection goes to the next node, waiting half a second and doubling up to ten seconds, with random jitter. [point at step 4] Only confirmed messages are written to confirmed.csv, which is the list the validator checks later.
slides.point: Step 1; in the code: confirm_delivery, delivery_mode=2, the two except blocks; then the bottom line and step 4.
slides.numbers: 5 = nack retry limit. 0.5 s to 10 s = reconnect backoff.
slides.proves: The producer implements publisher confirms, retries and node failover exactly as the assignment requires (real code from producer.py).
slides.transition: "[P4 name] will show how the consumer makes sure every confirmed message arrives."

slides.title: Consumer: manual acks, redelivery and idempotency
script: Thank you. Our consumer uses manual acknowledgements. [follow the flow] A message is delivered, parsed, checked against the IDs we have already seen, written to received.csv and flushed, and only then acknowledged.

If the consumer crashes before the ack, the broker gives the message to another consumer and marks it as redelivered. On an error we nack it back to the queue, and a delivery limit of ten stops a broken message from looping forever.

[point at the left box] Duplicates are normal with at-least-once delivery. Because we remember the IDs we have processed, a duplicate is acknowledged but not processed again. That makes the consumer idempotent.
[point at the right box] The validator subtracts received from confirmed. Anything left is lost, and the run fails.
slides.point: The five boxes left to right, the green basic_ack box, then the two lower boxes.
slides.proves: Manual acknowledgements, redelivery handling and idempotency are implemented, and loss is measured, not assumed.
slides.transition: "Now the results from our Docker cluster."

slides.title: Integration test on Docker: zero lost messages
script: We ran these tests ourselves on a Mac with Docker Desktop, with all three RabbitMQ containers healthy and Prometheus and Grafana running.
[point at the first card] The smoke test sent 10,000 messages: 10,000 confirmed by the broker, 10,000 received, nothing lost and no duplicates.

[point at the second card] Then we killed the queue leader while the producer and consumer were running. All 23,680 confirmed messages were received with zero loss. Two duplicates were delivered because of the crash, and our consumer did not process them twice. There were no ordering errors per consumer, and 95 percent of messages arrived within three milliseconds.
[point at the bottom row] To test more failure types we also ran a larger campaign on a native RabbitMQ test cluster with the same code: 24 failure runs, 467,287 messages, zero lost.
slides.point: First card; second card (23,680 / 23,680, 0 lost, 2 duplicates); then the bottom row and its label.
slides.numbers: 0 lost = every confirmed message arrived. 2 duplicates = redeliveries caused by the crash, removed by de-duplication. p95 2.96 ms = 95% of messages within 3 ms; max 513.79 ms = the failover moment.
slides.proves: End-to-end integration on our Docker deployment: producer, cluster, consumer and validator together lose nothing, even when the leader is killed.
slides.transition: "[P3 name] will show what happens inside the cluster during a leader crash."

slides.title: Fault tolerance: automatic leader election, no loss
script: This is one leader crash from our native test cluster, run 5, where every client was connected to the leader on purpose.

[point at the top screenshot] Before the crash, rabbit2 is the leader in Raft term 25. After it, rabbit1 is the leader in term 26: exactly one election, which took 521 milliseconds. All three nodes end with the same commit index, so the restarted node caught up from the log.
[point at the lower screenshot] The validator for the same run: 21,810 confirmed, 21,810 received, zero lost, and two redelivered duplicates handled.

[point at the table] Across all failure types, nothing was lost. Leader elections took about half a second, a partition was the slowest case at up to 28 seconds, and with two nodes down, writes stopped until a node returned. We chose consistency over availability.
slides.point: Top screenshot: the leader row moving from rabbit2 to rabbit1, Term 25 then 26, equal commit indexes. Lower screenshot: 21810 / 21810, LOST 0, RESULT PASS. Table: the Lost column.
slides.numbers: Term 25 to 26 = exactly one election. 521 ms = election time (from the run's scenario.log). Equal commit index = replicas back in sync. 28 s = slowest confirm pause, in a partition. 31-38 s = no writes without a majority.
slides.proves: Leader failover is automatic and loss-free, shown in Raft's own state and by the validator, and the table shows the same for every failure type.
slides.transition: "[P2 name] will show what this safety costs in performance."

slides.title: Performance: 33 benchmark runs, analysed
script: We ran 33 benchmark runs: eleven configurations, three times each, with the same safety settings as before.

[point at the bar chart] One producer thread sends about 315 messages per second, because it waits about 2 milliseconds for each Raft commit and confirm. Sixteen threads reach 774, limited by the two CPUs of the test machine.
[point at the line chart] Latency grows with load: the median from 2.3 to 13.3 milliseconds, and the 99th percentile to 74 at sixteen threads.

[point at the box] Large 64-kilobyte messages reached almost 20 megabytes per second, prefetch made no difference because the consumers were never the bottleneck, and the broker's own counters matched ours within 0.4 percent.
[point at Limitations] These numbers come from the native test cluster, not from our Docker Macs, so absolute values will differ there.
slides.point: Bar chart: 315 and 774. Line chart: the p99 line. Then the box and the Limitations text.
slides.numbers: 315 msg/s = one thread, limited by waiting for each confirm. 774 msg/s = sixteen threads. p99 74 ms = the slowest 1% under heavy load. 0.4% = agreement between broker and client counts.
slides.proves: Throughput and latency were measured and explained, not just reported, with clear limits.

slides.title: What we proved, and what we learned
script: To sum up. [point at Proved] No confirmed message was lost: not on Docker, and not in 24 native failure runs. Leaders were replaced automatically in about half a second.

[point at Learned] We learned that at-least-once delivery needs an idempotent consumer, that a partition is harder than a crash, and that a failover test only counts if the clients are on the node you kill.
Thank you. We are happy to take your questions.
slides.transition: All four answer questions; backup slides 11-14 are ready.
